questions.heading: A Prediction Describes the Future Without You; a Prescription Chooses What You Do
questions.stem: The asset model reports a cable section with an RUL of 2 years and a next-year PoF of 4%. A manager says it will fail within two years. What does the data say?

options.text: A 4% chance of failing within two years, since the PoF covers the RUL
options.says: The PoF here is for the next year only; it says nothing about a two-year window.

options.text: A 4% chance of failing in the next year, since the PoF covers one year
options.says: Right: PoF next year is the chance of a failure in the coming twelve months; RUL answers a different question.

options.text: A near-certain failure within two years, since the RUL counts down to failure
options.says: RUL is a separate model output and need not agree with the failure probability.

options.text: A near-certain failure in the next year, since the RUL is nearly spent
options.says: A low RUL is not a near-certain failure; the PoF says 4%.

questions.heading: Ranking by Risk Is Not a Plan
questions.stem: Funding the riskiest assets first until the money runs out claims to remove 30% more risk than the optimizer's plan, with the same budget and the same rules entered in the optimizer. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The ranking uses better coefficients, so its risk figures are more accurate
options.says: Both use the same coefficients; the ranking differs only in ignoring the rules.

options.text: The ranking's plan cannot be carried out, so its risk figure is not comparable
options.says: Right: a risk ranking knows the budget only, so it can fund two alternatives on one asset or skip a must-do.

options.text: The optimizer stopped before its best plan, so its answer is not optimal
options.says: An optimal solve cannot be beaten by a plan that obeys the same rules; the ranking does not obey them.

options.text: The optimizer maximizes the wrong quantity, so it removes less risk on purpose
options.says: The comparison is between plans scored on the same risk; the gap comes from the broken rules.

questions.heading: Predictions Enter the Model as Coefficients, and Their Errors Travel With Them
questions.stem: A review finds the PoF model may overstate transformer risk by up to 40%. Before adopting the plan, what should you check?

options.text: Re-fit the PoF model and see if its accuracy improves, since the model is what matters
options.says: Accuracy is the predictive model's measure; the planner needs to know if the decision is sensitive to the error.

options.text: Cut those PoFs by 40% and keep the current plan, since the plan was already optimal
options.says: Changing coefficients can change the optimal plan; only a re-solve tells you.

options.text: Compare each transformer's RUL with its PoF, since agreement between them shows accuracy
options.says: RUL and PoF need not agree, and their agreement says nothing about the plan's sensitivity.

options.text: Re-solve with those PoFs cut by 40% and see if the plan moves, since the decision is what matters
options.says: Right: if the plan is the same across the plausible error, the error does not matter for this decision.
